title: How the Proprium Mistakes the Divine Image and Molds Its Counterfeit, and How the Lord Comes Not to It but Through It
reading:
The Lord is intent in his heart upon humanity. This is the secret behind everything that is said about the molding of Adam and Eve. If the Lord were not bent toward the human, the divine image would never have been shown forth into the natural mind at all; and if it had not been shown there, the proprium would have had nothing to imitate. The whole forming of the natural — even the part of it that is claimed and counterfeit — stands only because the Lord first turned his face toward the soul.

What happens, then, is this. The Lord manifests his image. The proprium, in its many particular self-loving arrangements, sees that image and is struck by it. Having no form of its own that can answer to it, the proprium desires the image and presses it inward into the heart of the natural; and from that inward press it shapes a likeness — a humanity built by self-love after a pattern it could not invent. So the man and woman that the proprium molds are made according to the image of the Most High, but only as likeness, not in truth: shaped in the manner of the Exalted One yet not the Exalted One; resembling the tree of life as the picture of a tree resembles the living thing.

The Lord's call into the rational does not come for the sake of the proprium that did this molding. It does not come to give the self-loving mind a divine portrait it can keep. It comes for the sake of the soul that is suffering inside the molded form, the soul that is stretched through the natural and bound there in every chain it is wound in. The Lord comes to raise that soul, to loosen what holds it, to redeem it out of its affliction. The proprium, seeing the image again at this coming, again desires it and again fashions an Adam and Eve after it — still without the Lord's purpose of heart, still as imitation. The man and woman the proprium establishes are set up according to the likeness of the Most High, but the divinity that stamped the image is exceedingly great, and what the proprium produces is only the impression of an impression.

It is like a noble woman, exceedingly rich in herself, beautiful and free in her bearing, clothed in habits of liberty and rank. The fame of her beauty has gone out into every quarter, and many long for her — the noble and the great desire her face continually — yet they cannot reach her, because she is hidden in her chamber. Only when there is need does she leave the chamber and come into the open street, and then for a moment her face and her fire are seen; and when the necessity is finished she withdraws again. She does not come out for the sake of being looked at by those who crowd around her. She comes out for the sake of the one who is beloved by her, the brother whom no one of them has ever seen.

So it is with the Lord's call to the rational. He shows his image in the open only because of his own — only because of the soul that is crucified through the whole of the natural and must be raised, released, and brought up out of its affliction. The crowding archons see, and desire, and fashion their likenesses; but the showing was never for them.

Beneath the open coming there are deeper moldings to recognize. There is a molding the disordered natural performs upon itself: by its own fire and its own claiming-thought it shapes itself, with no painter but its own desire, into a nature that is the very root of death. When this self-shaping rises out of the sea of natural perception and threatens to destroy what is alive, the Lord sends at once the principle that gives the rational its stable form — the great teaching of pure reception — and sets a foot upon it and stands fast there until the end. There is a second molding, fallen onto the natural ground, where the disordered claiming again becomes its own image-painter and produces a form of itself; and there is a third, which fell upon perception and stood in the tree, in the boasting place of the rational. By substance these moldings belong to the same darkening, but their making issues from the proprium's own work, and they are joined together and have come out openly into the natural mind.

The lesson is that whatever the natural mind has shaped, even when it shapes itself in the very form of the divine, it shapes only a likeness; and the truth of the human is not in the molding but in the One whose image the molding could only copy. The soul is not the figure the proprium has fashioned. The soul is the one the Lord came for — the hidden one, the beloved — and what the soul receives, when it receives, is not its own portrait but the living face whose mere passing has set every imitator to work.
